extracted.intended_audience: British statesmen, legislators, and the politically engaged public (late-18th century)
extracted.subtask_description: A conservative political critique of the French Revolutionary reforms, assessing legitimacy, property, institutions, and prudent methods of reform. The text articulates standards for when and how governments may alter established social and property arrangements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sanctity of property and prescription
rubrics_metrics.description: We have never dreamt that Parliaments had any right whatever to violate property, to overrule prescription, or to force a currency of their own fiction in the place of that which is real, and recognized by the law of nations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Legislative assemblies ought not to set aside the rules of prescription or otherwise unsettle established property; if prescription is shaken, no species of property is secure. The text warns that permitting assemblies to ignore prescription makes property insecure and invites arbitrary confiscation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confiscation as a dangerous precedent (slippery slope)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is in the principle of injustice that the danger lies, and not in the description of persons on whom it is first exercised... I see the confiscators begin with bishops, and chapters, and monasteries; but I do not see them end there.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Confiscation, even if aimed at particular classes, threatens all property holders because it normalizes violation of rights; the practice will spread beyond initial targets to princes, landed estates, and the moneyed interest.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy accrues with time (prescription of government)
rubrics_metrics.description: This Assembly has hardly a year's prescription. To make a revolution is a measure which, primâ fronte, requires an apology. To make a revolution is to subvert the ancient state of our country; and no common reasons are called for to justify so violent a proceeding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Governments gain moral and legal standing through time and usage; revolutionary bodies lacking prescription must justify themselves and be scrutinized because they lack the settled authority that mellows legality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dangers of fanaticism and proselytism
rubrics_metrics.description: We cannot be ignorant of the spirit of atheistical fanaticism... These writings and sermons have filled the populace with a black and savage atrocity of mind... The spirit of proselytism attends this spirit of fanaticism.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rapid spread of extreme doctrines and organized proselytism can produce societal brutality, spread unrest across countries (examples: Munster, Berne), and should caution reformers against wholesale disruptive measures that inflame popular passions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve-and-improve rule (Spartam nactus es; hanc exorna)
rubrics_metrics.description: Spartam nactus es; hanc exorna. A man full of warm, speculative benevolence may wish his society otherwise constituted than he finds it; but a good patriot, and a true politician, always considers how he shall make the most of the existing materials of his country.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reformers should aim to adorn and improve existing institutions rather than destroy them outright. The standard for a statesman is both disposition to preserve and ability to improve; wholesale destruction is imprudent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberation and slowness as virtues in reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Without question it might [take many years]; and it ought. It is one of the excellences of a method in which time is amongst the assistants, that its operation is slow... If circumspection and caution are a part of wisdom, ... they become a part of duty too.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because institutions involve sentient beings and long habits, reforms should be slow and cautious; time helps avoid unintended misery caused by sudden changes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use existing institutional powers rather than selling them
rubrics_metrics.description: In the monastic institutions, in my opinion, was found a great 'power' for the mechanism of politic benevolence... There were revenues with a public direction; there were men wholly set apart and dedicated to public purposes...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monastic and corporate institutions supply enduring revenues, disciplined personnel, and objects (libraries, collections) suitable for long-term public projects; policymakers should harness these resources for public good instead of converting them into immediate private gain by sale.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare old possessors and proposed purchasers before transfer
rubrics_metrics.description: A sober legislator would carefully compare the possessor whom he was recommended to expel with the stranger who was proposed to fill his place... we ought to have some rational assurance that the purchasers ... will be in a considerable degree more laborious, more virtuous, more sober...
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Before confiscating or transferring property, assess the social, moral, and economic effects of the new owners' expenditure and behavior; do not assume that redistribution will improve industry or public morality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tolerance of certain superstitions may be preferable to destructive reforms
rubrics_metrics.description: Superstition is the religion of feeble minds; and they must be tolerated... perhaps he would think the superstition which builds to be more tolerable than that which demolishes,--that which adorns a country, than that which deforms it,--that which endows, than that which plunders.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Not all superstition should be eradicated if its presence sustains institutions that yield public goods (art, monuments, charity); reformers must weigh harms of superstition against harms of its removal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy must be indistinguishable from justice
rubrics_metrics.description: It is with the greatest difficulty that I am able to separate policy from justice. Justice is itself the great standing policy of civil society; and any eminent departure from it, under any circumstances, lies under the suspicion of being no policy at all.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good policy should align with justice; apparent short-term policy gains that require injustice are suspect and likely counterproductive in the long run.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid governing by untested speculation; ground reforms in experience
rubrics_metrics.description: They make this difference, because in their desire of obtaining and securing power they are thoroughly in earnest; there they travel in the beaten road. The public interests, because about them they have no real solicitude, they abandon wholly to chance... their schemes have nothing in experience to prove their tendency beneficial.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Public reforms should be based on experience and tested methods rather than on abstract theories and speculative schemes; abandoning experience risks misgovernance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Force is a poor substitute for wisdom
rubrics_metrics.description: With them defects in wisdom are to be supplied by the plenitude of force. They get nothing by it. Commencing their labors on a principle of sloth, they have the common fortune of slothful men.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When administrators lack wisdom, they may rely on coercive measures to achieve ends; this breeds arbitrary power and feeble, vicious results rather than genuine improvements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Corporate bodies are valuable long-term public instruments
rubrics_metrics.description: The perennial existence of bodies corporate and their fortunes are things particularly suited to a man who has long views... The institutions savor of superstition in their very principle; and they nourish it by a permanent and standing influence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Corporations and permanent institutions can be more easily directed for public purposes, hold collections and revenues for posterity, and are therefore important assets for prudent statesmanship rather than nuisances to be abolished.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reform requires confronting difficulty, not evading it
rubrics_metrics.description: Difficulty is a severe instructor... He that wrestles with us strengthens our nerves and sharpens our skill... This amicable conflict with difficulty obliges us to an intimate acquaintance with our object.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Effective statesmanship demands engaging and working through hard problems; avoiding difficulty leads to superficial solutions and eventual failure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Destruction without constructive plan yields feeble insecure systems
rubrics_metrics.description: They have commenced their schemes of reform with abolition and total destruction... Rage and frenzy will pull down more in half an hour than prudence, deliberation, and foresight can build up in a hundred years.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Criticism and demolition require far less skill than constructive reform; sweeping abolition often leaves a vacuum filled by worse arrangements unless a thoughtful, practicable plan is prepared.
